Subject: ParkAvon capacity recommendation: memory vs throughput tradeoffs for Dedicated pool

Hi Ethan —

Thanks for the call this morning. Per our discussion we sketched three candidate Dedicated fleet options for your inferred workloads and wanted to capture the tradeoffs to help you decide before Procurement locks down the SKU on the SOW. High level notes below; attached is a one‑page perf summary and a CSV of the small-scale benchmarks we ran against a sample of the ParkAvon request mix.

Summary recommendations (short):
- H100 primary (mixed-precision) for long-context agents and fine-tuned models (best latency for 32k+ contexts, largest KV cache headroom).
- A100 pool for high-throughput synchronous inference (batching favorable; lower per-token latency at scale for 8k-16k contexts when batched).
- L4 workers for embedding-heavy background workloads and lower-cost burst capacity (best cost/token for short-context, non-KV use).

Key tradeoffs to consider:
- Memory headroom: H100 > A100 > L4 (important for multi-turn state and large KV caches).
- Single-request latency (cold-start): H100 slightly better for long-context; A100 benefits more from batching.
- Unit economics: L4 < A100 < H100 for per-token cost in typical short-context flows.
- Fallback and routing: we recommend an autoscale + tiered routing policy so real-time traffic uses H100/A100 and embeddings fall to L4.

Ask from you: can you confirm typical 95th-percentile concurrent requests during peak and the fraction of flows that require >16k context? We used the sample traffic you shared but want to align our final SOW SKU counts to your peak.

Next steps: Aditya will capture this in a short ops runbook and Markus will weigh-in on fallback/slotting rules. If you want a formal mutual action plan, we can generate that after we align on peak concurrency.

Thanks —
Stephanie Nguyen
Account Executive, Redwood Inference

Stephanie —

Thanks, this is helpful. A couple clarifying Qs from my side:
1) Peak concurrency: we expect intermittent bursts up to ~280 concurrent inference threads (95p) but typical sustained is ~60. Bursts are short (minutes).
2) Long-context fraction: about 12% of our traffic touches >16k contexts (mainly research/QA flows); the rest are 2k-4k.
3) Question on mixing: would you recommend a pure-H100 reserved pool for SLA, or a mixed reserve + on-demand L4 / A100 for bursts? Cost is a concern if we reserve large H100 capacity.

Also Procurement wanted to know if you can call out any mitigations so we don't need to over-provision H100 for rare long-context peaks.

—Ethan

Ethan —

Appreciate the numbers — that helps a lot. With 12% >16k contexts and 95p bursts to ~280 concurrent, my practical recommendation is:

- Reserve a baseline H100 fleet sized for your sustained long-context capacity + small safety margin (cover ~120 concurrent long-context slots).
- Add a reserved A100 pool sized to handle baseline synchronous throughput (cover ~80 concurrent mid-length requests with batching headroom).
- Configure L4 as burstable capacity (on-demand + a small reserved slot for predictable background embedding jobs).

Mitigations to avoid over-reserving H100:
- Routing + graceful degradation: implement a policy where, if H100 is saturated, best-effort long-context requests fall back to an A100 variant with quantization and reduced KV history (we can keep a degraded state that retains 8–12k of context).
- Prefetch/caching: for repeat query patterns we can warm KV caches so long-context requests hit cached prefixes.
- Autoscale + burst credits: Redwood Dedicated supports short burst capacity above reserved levels for a reduced premium — this covers minute-scale spikes without full reservation.

I attached the benchmark CSV showing latency/throughput by SKU for sample traces you gave — the data supports the mixed-pool approach for cost-efficiency. Also attached a draft pricing workbook that maps reserve sizes to monthly spend.

If that approach works, Aditya will draft the slot counts and margin assumptions into the SOW. Markus — can you add ops-level fallthrough suggestions?

Thanks,
Stephanie
Account Executive, Redwood Inference
[Attachments: benchmaks_peak_concurrency.csv, parkavon_pricing_v2.xlsx]

Team —

Notes for the SOW and runbook:
- Fleet mix: target 12 H100 slots (N effective) to cover the 120 long-context concurrent target if you assume ~10 active sessions per slot depending on model param/kv sizing. Exact slot math in the spreadsheet.
- A100 pool: provision ~10 A100 slots to handle batched mid-length queries with headroom for concurrency bursts. A100 gives better batched throughput for GPT-style decoders at mid-context lengths.
- L4 pool: keep 6 baseline L4 instances reserved for embeddings and background jobs; enable burstable L4 on-demand for sudden volume.
- Fallback rules: set H100->A100 fallthrough with auto-quantize flag and limit KV to 12k tokens when falling back. Track percentage of fallbacks in telemetry and alert at 5% sustained.
- Autoscale policy: aggressive scale-up for <2min bursts using spot-on-demand mix, conservative scale-down to avoid flapping.
- DR/region: keep mirrored pools in us-east-1 and us-west-2 for failover; cross-region failover only for degraded throughput.

I'll add exact GPU-hour estimates and the pricing buckets; Aditya, can you fold this into the SOW and align with Procurement about burst credits?

-Markus
